items.title: Cedar Walton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: When I heard, not too long ago, a version of Cherokee with him and uh organist Jimmy Smith, uh I couldn't believe how he got through those changes, you know, knowing him and his knowledge of, of uh harmony.

ctx.x: Uh, if you could – and I'm stepping out of chronology now – but just talk about them as trombone players.

Well, just uh basically Curtis' musical knowledge uh didn't quite add up to J.J.'s but he compensated by havin' a larger sound. And by large I just mean large. It was … J.J.'s had, his sound was adequate. I mean, more than adequate, mind you, but for some reason, somehow Curtis found a way to make his bigger. I don't know whether it was the mouthpiece, the embrasure or what. Uh, just the, the, the, uh physical uh attributes of his being, you know. But uh, I always thought that, but he didn't uh, he didn't have…
So you're saying that J.J. was stronger theoretically.
